generated.script:
A: On our arts and environment programme today, I'm joined by Tom Fletcher, a landscape architect who's been steering a project to turn an old canal basin into a wetland park. Tom, how did you end up heading this scheme?
B: Well, the council actually came to our practice — they'd seen what we'd done with a former railway siding in Leeds, turning it into a pocket park. This basin had been fenced off for years, basically a dumping ground, and they wanted something that would pull people back to the waterfront without pretending the industrial past hadn't happened.
A: What kind of reaction did you get when you first presented the plans?
B: Honestly? People were less bothered about losing a few parking spots than we expected. What kept coming up in the consultation was smell and mosquitoes — as if we'd be creating a swamp in the middle of the city. We had to keep explaining that a properly designed wetland actually filters water rather than letting it sit and go stagnant.
A: And the planting — how did you decide what to put in?
B: We stuck with native species throughout, partly because they're built to cope with the heavy metals still lurking in the soil. There's an industrial legacy here, so we'd have been foolish to ship in exotic plants that look pretty but don't survive. The idea was to set up habitats that dragonflies and small fish could move into within a couple of seasons.
A: You've relied quite heavily on volunteers, haven't you?
B: Yeah, and I'll admit I didn't think we'd fill every muddy Saturday session. We've had retired engineers, university students, even a few teenagers who initially turned up for something to put on their applications — though plenty of them kept coming back once they got stuck in. It's knackering work, but there's something satisfying about seeing a bare edge turn green within weeks.
A: Funding hasn't all been straightforward though?
B: We had to trim back one of the boardwalk sections when a national grant fell through — that was a blow. The capital phase is more or less done now, but keeping the pumps and planting maintained is going to depend on continued council backing, and I don't take that for granted given how budgets get reshuffled every year.
A: Have schools made use of the space?
B: Absolutely — biology groups come down throughout the year to sample water quality and track which birds have moved in. We did put safety rails along the deeper channels, but it's not a playground with swings; it's deliberately a place where you observe rather than charge around.
A: If you could press ahead with one thing, what would it be?
B: I'd love to extend the wetland footprint along the rest of the canal that's still choked with reed and rubbish. We've proved the model works here — why stop at one basin when you could stitch a whole corridor together for wildlife and walkers alike?
A: Tom Fletcher, thank you for talking to us.
